summary: Atari Games/Midway stunt-racing series beginning with San Francisco arcade racers and later expanding to futuristic and open-world street-racing entries.

entries.title: San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing
entries.definitive_edition: Nintendo 64 home version plus PlayStation secondary content

emulation.notes: Use N64 emulation for the primary route, PlayStation emulation for the secondary content, and MAME for arcade reference.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: High-resolution N64 emulation plus PlayStation side content

primary.why: The original arcade release has the core three-track arcade game, while the Nintendo 64 version adds more tracks, hidden content, practice, death race, circuit mode, saving, and multiplayer-friendly home play. The PlayStation version has its own bonus track and modes, so it is preserved as a secondary route.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Nintendo 64 version in a high-resolution N64 emulator; use PlayStation emulation only for the exclusive bonus-track/mode content.

secondary.exclusive_content: Exclusive bonus track plus GP and Explosive modes.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the bonus track and the two PlayStation-exclusive modes.
secondary.why: The PlayStation conversion has sourced unique content but fewer tracks and changed presentation compared with the N64 route.

entries.remaster_caveats: The Rock/Alcatraz update is tracked as its own entry because it adds major arcade content.

entries.title: San Francisco Rush The Rock: Alcatraz Edition

emulation.emulator: MAME / original hardware / Glide-capable PC setup
emulation.notes: Use arcade preservation for the main route; the PC pack-in is best treated as archival hardware history.

primary.version: San Francisco Rush: The Rock: Wave Net
primary.why: The Rock update added tracks, shortcuts, cars, and a mirror option; the later WaveNet arcade revision added networked multiplayer support. That makes the WaveNet cabinet the most complete arcade route, while the PC release was a rare hardware pack-in.
primary.how_to_play: Use a supported arcade setup or MAME-compatible route for The Rock/WaveNet where available; preserve the PC Quantum3D Raven version only as a hardware-specific curiosity.

entries.remaster_caveats: No modern remaster is sourced; later Midway Arcade Treasures collections include The Rock as a compilation route.

entries.title: Rush 2: Extreme Racing USA

emulation.notes: Use high-resolution N64 emulation; original hardware remains the reference route.

primary.why: Rush 2 is sourced as a Nintendo 64 exclusive and adds multiple U.S. city tracks, a proper stunt track, hidden shortcuts, jumps, and unlockable content.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Nintendo 64 release in a high-resolution N64 emulator with a controller profile tuned for analog steering.

entries.remaster_caveats: No remaster or later port is sourced.

entries.title: San Francisco Rush 2049
entries.definitive_edition: Dreamcast home version plus arcade Tournament/Special Edition side content

emulation.notes: Use Flycast for the Dreamcast primary route; MAME for arcade update content; N64/GBC emulation only for comparison.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: High-resolution Dreamcast emulation plus arcade update content

primary.why: Rush 2049's home versions add stunt wings, battle mode, obstacle-course content, stunt arenas, and battle venues; the Dreamcast version is the strongest full home-console route. The arcade Special/Tournament Edition content has additional tracks/cars, so arcade remains a secondary preservation route.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Dreamcast version in Flycast or on Dreamcast; then sample the arcade Special/Tournament Edition content through arcade preservation if available.

secondary.exclusive_content: Tournament/Special Edition arcade variants with additional tracks, additional cars, and fixes.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the added arcade tracks/cars in the Tournament or Special Edition cabinet versions.
secondary.why: The home versions add modes and wings, but the rarer arcade updates include their own sourced additions.

entries.remaster_caveats: Midway Arcade Treasures compilation releases are reissue routes, not new definitive remasters; some licensed advertisements were changed in compilation releases.

entries.title: L.A. Rush

emulation.notes: Use PC as primary; console and PSP emulation are fallback routes.

primary.why: L.A. Rush released for PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2005, then Windows and PSP in 2006. The Windows version has the highest output ceiling for the open-world entry, and no sourced platform-exclusive mission content requires a secondary playthrough.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Windows release on a compatibility setup; use Xbox or PlayStation 2 emulation as fallback, and PSP only for the portable Rush variant.

entries.remaster_caveats: No remaster is sourced; a planned Gizmondo version was canceled.

entries.title: San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing / The Rock: Alcatraz Edition
entries.definitive_edition: Nintendo 64 main route plus arcade/PlayStation secondary checks

emulation.notes: Use N64 emulation for the main route; use MAME/arcade hardware and DuckStation only for secondary content.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: N64 upscaling for content-rich route, arcade emulation for cabinet fidelity

primary.why: The original arcade Rush released in 1996 and was expanded by The Rock: Alcatraz Edition and WaveNet. The Nintendo 64 version adds home modes, hidden keys/vehicles, secret stunt content, save support, and tracks derived from the original and The Rock, making it the best single main route despite the arcade version's cabinet fidelity.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Nintendo 64 version through Ares/ParaLLEl-RDP or original hardware for the main run; sample The Rock/WaveNet arcade versions and the PlayStation version for their exclusive arcade/port-specific content.

secondary.exclusive_content: The Rock: Alcatraz Edition and WaveNet arcade cabinet versions with arcade-specific Alcatraz/cabinet/network presentation.
secondary.what_to_play: Sample The Rock/WaveNet arcade versions for the cabinet handling and arcade-only network/cabinet experience.
secondary.why: The N64 version is the most practical complete home route, but the arcade revisions preserve the original cabinet context.

secondary.exclusive_content: PlayStation port with an exclusive bonus track plus GP and Explosive modes.
secondary.what_to_play: Play the PlayStation-exclusive track and modes only.
secondary.why: The PlayStation version is lower fidelity and has fewer tracks than the N64 route, but its bonus track/modes are sourced exclusives.

entries.remaster_caveats: Midway Arcade Treasures compilations preserve The Rock access but do not replace the N64 home-content route.

entries.title: Rush 2: Extreme Racing USA

emulation.notes: Use modern N64 emulation for upscaled play or original hardware for native timing.

primary.why: Rush 2 was released exclusively for Nintendo 64, adding U.S. city/state courses, two-player play, Rumble Pak support, hidden shortcuts/jumps, and unlockable content.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Nintendo 64 version through Ares/ParaLLEl-RDP or original hardware.

entries.remaster_caveats: No sourced remaster or complete edition.

entries.title: San Francisco Rush 2049
entries.definitive_edition: Dreamcast release plus arcade/GBC secondary checks

emulation.notes: Use Dreamcast emulation for the main route, arcade emulation for cabinet revisions, and GBC emulation for the handheld adaptation.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Dreamcast home fidelity plus arcade cabinet preservation

primary.why: Rush 2049 began as an arcade game and was ported to Dreamcast, Nintendo 64, Game Boy Color, and later compilations. The Dreamcast version is the strongest home route for the 3D console content, including stunt wings and the robust race/stunt/battle structure, while arcade revisions and the Game Boy Color version preserve distinct content/presentation.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Dreamcast version through Flycast/Redream or original hardware; sample arcade Tournament/Special Edition cabinets and the Game Boy Color version for their exclusive presentation/content.

secondary.exclusive_content: Arcade/Tournament/Special Edition cabinet versions with force-feedback cabinet controls, PIN progression, and arcade revision content.
secondary.what_to_play: Sample the arcade versions for cabinet handling and revision-specific tracks/cars.
secondary.why: Dreamcast is the best home main route, but the arcade versions preserve the original cabinet experience.

secondary.exclusive_content: Top-down handheld version with tracks that differ from the 3D versions.
secondary.what_to_play: Sample the GBC track set and top-down adaptation.
secondary.why: The GBC release is a distinct handheld interpretation, not a substitute for Dreamcast.

entries.remaster_caveats: Midway Arcade Treasures versions are compilation access routes; arcade Tournament/Special Edition content should be checked separately if cabinet completeness matters.

entries.title: L.A. Rush / Rush
entries.definitive_edition: Windows PC release plus PSP Stunt Arena check

emulation.notes: Use Windows for the main route and PPSSPP for the PSP-specific Stunt Arena route.
emulation.fidelity_ceiling: Windows PC route for main fidelity, PPSSPP for secondary mode

primary.why: L.A. Rush released for PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2005, then Windows and PlayStation Portable as Rush in 2006. Windows is the highest-fidelity main route for the open-world Los Angeles entry, while PSP includes the Stunt Arena mode not present on the home versions.
primary.how_to_play: Play the Windows version at the highest stable settings for the main run; sample the PSP version for Stunt Arena mode.

secondary.exclusive_content: PSP version titled Rush with Stunt Arena mode and Wi-Fi-supported cruise missions.
secondary.what_to_play: Play Stunt Arena and sample PSP-specific connected cruise content if available.
secondary.why: Windows is the better main-fidelity route, but PSP has sourced mode/content differences.

entries.remaster_caveats: No sourced remaster. The planned Gizmondo port was cancelled and is not counted as a release.
